NATURE CLUB CLASS · ANIMALS

The deeper animal deck.

Twenty-two spotter sheets walk the wild in study order — the birds first, then the water from shore to deep, the small crews that run the world, the fur families and their famous cousins, and the wild homes of six habitats — and every tile below is a kid-followable guide, right on this page.

HOW THIS CLASS WORKS

Every animal group — with a spotter lesson on its card.

The Nature Club Animals class is the deeper deck: where Animal Categories teaches the big families, this one goes specialist — birds of prey, crustaceans, pollinators, the dog family, rodents, and the wild homes from grassland to mountaintop. Twenty-two spotter sheets, each with four labeled animals, and each card opens a simple lesson a kid can follow: what the group is, who belongs, how to tell the look-alikes apart, and one way to spot them on a real walk.

The walks run in study order on purpose. The birds come first — hunters before singers; then the water, from the shore to the deep; then the small crews that run the world; the fur families with their famous cousins; and the wild homes, six addresses from grassland to cave to mountaintop. The age pills lean Ages 4–5 on purpose too: this is the step-up deck, and the friendliest five cards ride Ages 3+ for confident younger spotters.

THE CLASS GAME

The Spotter’s Walk: one card, one walk, one met animal.

Take one card on your walk — garden-birds on any day, birds-of-prey for the park with the big trees, river-animals for the stream. The job is simple: spot ONE real creature that belongs to the card’s family, and watch it long enough to say one true thing about it. At home, draw what you met next to the card version and write the date. A notebook of met animals is the Nature Club badge of honor — one page per walk, no rush, and the deck decides where next week’s walk goes.

SAME ANIMAL, TWO NAMES

Reindeer and caribou. Both are right.

Animals carry their names across oceans like passports — and this class says so out loud. The reindeer of Lapland is the caribou of Canada and Alaska — same animal, two names. The moose is called the elk in Britain. A shrimp in America is a prawn in Britain. And the buzzard is the trickiest of all: in North America it means a vulture, but in Britain it means a hawk — one word, two birds, and this class teaches both. Whichever your family says, your child hears both — and learns early that animals, like words, come in kinds.

Age ranges are a guide, not a test. The age pill on every card is an honest hint: this is the deeper deck, so most cards ride Ages 4–5 — but the friendliest groups (garden birds, the seashore, the river, the pollinators, the dog family) ride Ages 3+. Start where your child’s curiosity already points; the card in their hand is always the right card.

TEACHER’S LESSON

How this class is taught.

By the end of this class: your child has met all 22 cards in Nature Club Animals, said each word with you and tried one small activity from the lesson.

  1. 01
    Welcome

    “Hello! Today we are learning about Nature Club Animals. We have 22 cards, and we will look at them one at a time.”

    How: Sit side by side with the cards in front of you. Keep your voice warm and unhurried, and let your child touch the cards.

  2. Cards 1–10
  3. 02
    Card 1 · Birds of Prey

    “Birds of prey! They hunt with their eyes and their feet. The eagle is the giant, the hawk circles round and round, the falcon is the fastest animal on Earth when it dives, and the osprey catches fish straight out of the water — splash!”

    How: Hawk eyes minute: sit by a window and find three tiny things a hawk might spot from the sky — a coin, a leaf, a crack in the path. Sharp eyes are the hunting tool; practice is the game.

  4. 03
    Card 2 · Garden Birds

    “Garden birds! The robin hops close to see who you are, the woodpecker taps the tree — tok-tok-tok — the blue jay squawks the news, and the cardinal is the reddest bird in the yard. Who is visiting YOUR feeder today?”

    How: Counting feeder: fill a simple feeder (or scatter seeds) and keep a tally with stickers — one per bird visit. Which card bird shows up most? Real bird counts like this help real scientists, too.

  5. 04
    Card 3 · Desert Birds

    “Desert birds! The roadrunner runs — beep beep! — faster than most birds fly, the desert owl naps in the shade all day, the vulture rides the warm wind round and round, and the sandgrouse flies far to bring water home in its belly feathers!”

    How: Roadrunner relay: race across the yard on foot — running style only, wings optional. Then float around the room with still arms like a vulture riding the hot wind, without a single flap.

  6. 05
    Card 4 · Australian Birds

    “Australian birds! The emu is taller than a grown-up and runs instead of flying, the kookaburra laughs at the sky — ha-ha-ha — the cassowary wears a hard helmet, and the lyrebird can copy car alarms, chainsaws and other birds, perfectly!”

    How: Kookaburra song: learn the old song "Kookaburra sits in the old gum tree" and try your best laugh-call. Then play copycat like the lyrebird: repeat every sound the leader makes for one whole minute.

  7. 06
    Card 5 · Coastal Animals

    “Coastal animals! The seal slides on its belly, the sea lion claps and barks, the pelican scoops fish in its pouch — scoop! — and the puffin flies underwater with its wings. The beach is their kitchen!”

    How: Beach moves: wriggle like a seal on a rug, walk on all fours and bark like a sea lion, stretch your arms into a pouch and scoop a "fish" from the blue carpet, then flap-splash like a puffin.

  8. 07
    Card 6 · River Animals

    “River animals! The otter plays and slides all day, the beaver builds a house of sticks — slap goes its tail! The river dolphin swims in the big slow rivers, and the crocodile floats like a log with eyes. Careful stepping, crocodile territory!”

    How: Otter slide: socks on a smooth floor, run and slide — otters slide for fun, that is the whole lesson. Then build a "dam" of cushions that actually holds back a wave of rolled socks.

  9. 08
    Card 7 · Wetland Animals

    “Wetland animals! The heron stands like a statue — one fish, please! The stork struts on stilts, the alligator glides with just its eyes above the water, and the muskrat paddles its own little boat of a body. Shhh — the marsh is listening.”

    How: Heron statue game: freeze like a hunting heron for ten whole seconds, then snap your neck forward to catch a sock-fish. The stillness is the skill — and it is harder than it sounds.

  10. 09
    Card 8 · Crustaceans

    “Crustaceans! Shells on the outside, legs everywhere. The lobster has a big crusher claw and a small snipper claw, the shrimp snaps backwards to escape, the crayfish hides under river rocks, and the barnacle stands on its head in one spot forever!”

    How: Crab-walk tag: scuttle sideways, and when tagged, freeze in a shrimp-tail curl. Count the legs on a toy crab or shrimp — ten walking legs, plus claws. Too many legs is the family trademark.

  11. 10
    Card 9 · Shellfish

    “Shellfish! Animals with shells instead of bones. The clam hides in the sand and spits little fountains, the mussels hold hands with threads to stay on the rocks, the oyster makes pearls from sand it did not want, and the nautilus is a spiral shell with a tentacled pilot inside!”

    How: Shell sorting bowl: mix clean shells (or pasta shells) and sort by spiral, fan and flat. Open a real mussel shell and find the hinge — every shellfish shell has its own closing trick.

  12. 11
    Card 10 · Deep-Sea Animals

    “Deep-sea animals! Down where the sun cannot reach, it is dark — so some animals make their own light! The anglerfish dangles a glowing fishing rod, the giant squid has the biggest eyes in the animal kingdom, the manta ray flaps like a giant bird, and the sea turtle swims across the whole ocean and finds its way home.”

    How: Glow-in-the-dark angler: tape a small battery tea-light to a rod or stick, dim the room, and fish for paper fish with paperclip mouths. The glow-in-the-dark trick is how real anglers hunt in the dark.

  13. Cards 11–20
  14. 12
    Card 11 · Pollinators

    “Pollinators! They visit flowers for a sweet drink and carry the yellow dust — pollen — to the next flower, and that is how fruit begins! The honeybee dances the directions, the bumblebee buzzes in the cold morning, the hummingbird sips while hovering, and the bat does the night shift.”

    How: Pollination tag: tape paper "pollen dots" to your child’s fingers, and move them from flower cup to flower cup — every transfer makes a fruit sticker appear. Bees really do dance: watch a short video of the waggle dance together.

  15. 13
    Card 12 · Invertebrates

    “Invertebrates! Animals with no bones inside — some wear shells instead, and some are just squishy and strong. The octopus is the smartest animal without a spine, the earthworm makes the garden grow, the snail carries its house everywhere, and the starfish pulls itself along on hundreds of tiny feet.”

    How: No-bones day: move across the room like each invertebrate — slither like a worm, glide slow like a snail, stretch five arms like a starfish, and curl your arms into eight "tentacles" like an octopus. Bones optional; imagination not.

  16. 14
    Card 13 · Spiders & Ticks

    “Spiders and ticks! Eight legs, two body parts, no antennae — arachnids! The spider spins silk from its own body, the tarantula wears fuzzy pants, the tick waits patiently in the grass, and the harvestman strolls by on stilt legs.”

    How: Web engineering: wind wool or string between chair legs into a web with at least three sizes of gap, then toss pom-pom "bugs" — which gap catches? Silk is stronger than steel of the same weight: say it out loud, then test it.

  17. 15
    Card 14 · The Dog Family

    “The dog family! Wolves live in family packs and howl at the moon — arooooo! The coyote is clever and quick, the arctic fox grows a white coat for winter, and the dingo is the wild dog of Australia. Your puppy at home? Same big family, smallest member!”

    How: Pack howl: the family howls together, one at a time then all at once — wolves howl to say "we are here, all together." Then walk a "patrol" around the yard like coyotes, staying exactly together.

  18. 16
    Card 15 · Deer & Grazers

    “Deer and grazers! They eat grass and leaves all day and run fast. The moose is huge with a wide antler crown, the reindeer pulls sleds through the snow, the bison is a big brown wall of fur, and the antelope bounces like the grass is a trampoline!”

    How: Grazer lunch: try grazing like a real herbivore — a plate of spinach leaves, celery and carrots, eaten slowly, grazing-style. Then gallop in place like an antelope while a grown-up moose-calls: a low "muuuh" from the cupped hands.

  19. 17
    Card 16 · Rodents

    “Rodents! Their teeth grow and grow, so they gnaw and gnaw — that is the whole family trick! The squirrel buries acorns, the porcupine says ‘don’t touch‘ with its quills, the chinchilla is the softest animal you can name, and the prairie dog kisses its neighbors hello in the tunnel town!”

    How: Tooth-truth demo: find what a pencil, an acorn and a cardboard box have in common — rodents can chew all three. Then build a "prairie dog town" of tunnels from cushions and take turns popping up with a hello kiss (air kiss, prairie-dog style).

  20. 18
    Card 17 · African Grassland Animals

    “African grassland animals! The lion naps in the shade — even kings need naps! The cheetah runs as fast as a car on the highway, the wildebeest walks in herds bigger than a whole town, and the ostrich is a bird that sprints — and lays the biggest egg on Earth!”

    How: Grassland sprint test: measure a straight course, run it three times like a cheetah, then try ostrich style — big strides, wings tucked. Then lie in the shade like a lion and count who is breathing hardest.

  21. 19
    Card 18 · South American Animals

    “South American animals! The llama carries loads up the mountains, the sloth does everything in slow motion, the jaguar swims AND climbs, and the capybara — a guinea pig the size of a dog! — gets along with every animal in the river.”

    How: Capybara hot spring: fill a basin with warm water, and every toy in the house is invited — capybaras famously share their baths with anyone. Then a llama obstacle walk: carry a small backpack across a cushion trail without dropping it.

  22. 20
    Card 19 · More Arctic Animals

    “More arctic animals! The arctic hare wears a white coat in winter and brown in summer, the snowy owl hunts even when the sun never sets, the musk ox huddles in a circle with its family, and the arctic tern flies from the top of the world to the bottom and back — every single year!”

    How: Coat-change game: one side of the room is summer (brown scarf), the other winter (white scarf) — run and change coats as the caller switches seasons. Then a migration flight: cross the room twice without landing, like the tern does over whole oceans.

  23. 21
    Card 20 · Cave Animals

    “Cave animals! No sunlight down here — ever! The bat flies by listening to echoes, the salamander has skin the color of the pale moon, the cave cricket hops without seeing, and the olm is white as a ghost, blind as a stone, and can live for a hundred years!”

    How: Echo location: one person closes their eyes and calls "where am I?", and the other answers from a new spot — the listener points. Bats "see" with sound exactly this way. Then draw what you think the olm looks like before checking the card.

  24. Cards 21–22
  25. 22
    Card 21 · Mountain Animals

    “Mountain animals! Up where the air is thin and the rocks are steep. The mountain goat climbs sheer cliffs like stairs, the snow leopard balances with its giant fluffy tail, the yak walks through snow like it is nothing, and the marmot whistles — tweet! — to say ‘eagle overhead!‘”

    How: Balance-beak mountain: walk a line of tape on the floor with arms up like a snow leopard’s tail — the balance is the trick. Then a marmot whistle drill: one person hides a toy and whistles twice; the finder locates it.

  26. 23
    Card 22 · More Mountain Animals

    “More mountain animals! The ibex has horns curved like bananas, the chamois bounces from rock to rock — boing! — the pika squeaks from its haystack, and the condor flies with wings wider than a car without flapping once!”

    How: Haystack relay: like the pika, collect "hay" (balls of paper) from one side of the room and stack a winter pile on the other — against a timer. Then glide with still arms from wall to wall like a condor: no flapping allowed.

  27. 24
    Practice

    “Now you are the teacher! Pick any card and tell me what it is.”

    How: Let your child choose the card and say the word in their own way. Teaching someone else is the strongest way to remember.

  28. 25
    Check

    “Can you find Birds of Prey? Now show me Invertebrates.”

    How: A point, a fetch or the word all count as a pass. If they are unsure, name it for them and try again another day — there are no scores and no pressure.

  29. 26
    Well done

    “Well done! Today we met 22 cards. Let us look for one of them at home.”

    How: End on a win, then spot one of the words in real life today. Meeting it again in the real world is what makes it stay.

Read the script while you show the cards — the say-lines are yours to say out loud and the how-lines are the activity behind each step. Skip, shorten or repeat anything: the class bends to your child, never the other way round.
